Out in a shared space like the garden, comfort starts with simple, predictable habits that signal respect. I’m a big believer in clear house rules everyone can live with—posted right where people can see them—so we don’t have to guess what’s okay: keep music to a reasonable hour, pick up after yourself, share tools fairly, no aggressive behavior, no drinking or drugs on site. When everybody knows the boundaries, folks can relax.

Beyond rules, it’s the small courtesies that do the heavy lifting. Learn and use the name someone gives you. If you’re unsure how to say it, ask and try. Don’t assume who’s married to whom or what someone believes—say “partner” unless told otherwise, let people introduce their own story. If a neighbor’s English is limited, slow down, use simple words, point, smile; don’t raise your voice like they’re hard of hearing. If someone’s religious practice affects time or food, we can work around it—schedule cleanups with options, label potluck dishes plainly, no pressure for anyone to join in what isn’t theirs.

When it comes to folks struggling with alcohol or substances, lead with compassion and firm boundaries. I won’t judge a person for what they’re fighting, but I won’t pretend there aren’t lines: no using on site, no showing up impaired if it puts others at risk, and if someone needs help, we point them to resources and check in privately rather than call them out in front of a crowd. Same principle with health issues, including infectious ones: respect privacy, don’t play armchair doctor, follow basic hygiene—wash hands, wipe tools, stay home if you’re sick—and if a neighbor shares a need (“I’d prefer gloves” or “I tire easily”), we accommodate without drama.

There are places where extra communication and tolerance go a long way:
- Shared schedules and space: Garden beds, hoses, and pathways create friction when people assume. A simple sign-up sheet for water times or tool borrowing cuts down on the “you jumped the line” feeling that sets folks off.
- Noise and family routines: Kids run, grandparents need quiet, some folks work nights. A posted quiet window and a friendly reminder—“Hey, can we wrap the music by 8?”—beats resentment.
- Cultural misunderstandings: A holiday firecracker or a prayer ritual might surprise someone. A heads-up—“We’ll have guests Friday evening for a celebration”—and a willingness to explain or ask curious, respectful questions reduces fear and gossip.
- Safety concerns: If someone’s behavior starts to feel unsafe, it helps to have a calm, agreed process—two neighbors speak privately, offer options (“take a break, get some water”), and if it keeps up, step away and loop in the organizer. No yelling, no shaming.

Why more talk and tolerance? Because most blowups aren’t about values; they’re about surprises, stress, or folks feeling invisible. When money’s tight or jobs are shaky, people get protective over small things—time slots, tools, the bit of ground they tend—because they don’t control much else. When someone’s new or different, the unknown makes us fill in the blanks with our own stories, and those aren’t always kind. A little context—names, routines, what to expect—takes the temperature down. And tolerance doesn’t mean anything goes; it means we judge behavior, not backstory.

Bottom line for me: be a good neighbor in the ordinary ways—show up on time, say please and thank you, clean your mess, offer help without making a show of it, and take correction without getting prickly. Make space for people to be themselves, and set firm, fair lines so everyone feels safe. If we keep our eyes on those basics, folks from all walks can settle in and feel like they belong.

Fairness also means the big guys don’t get to write their own rules while the little guys foot the bill. If I pay my taxes and follow the law, the outfit up the hill ought to do the same.

Belonging, for me, is when you can walk into the hardware store and somebody knows your name, and you know theirs. It’s being able to afford to stay in the neighborhood where you’ve got roots. It’s hearing your voice matter at a school board meeting, even if you’re not fancy. I learned the hard way what belonging means when I moved for work in my forties—felt like an outsider until a neighbor showed up with a snow shovel after the first storm and said, “You’re on Maple now; we look out for each other.” That stuck. Belonging is offered, but you also earn it: you show up, you pitch in, you learn the rhythm of the place.

Community is the day-to-day stuff: checking on Mrs. Patel when her porch light stays on too long, coaching Little League even when you’re dog-tired, bringing a casserole to a family after a layoff. It’s also holding each other to standards—if your dog’s tearing up the garden or your kid’s being a knucklehead, someone tells you straight and you take it. I’ve got folks in my family who wrestled with drinking; that taught me compassion without pretending consequences don’t exist. Community works best when we share a few basics—speak to each other respectfully, pull your weight, and remember we’re neighbors first and everything else second. You can disagree about politics at the diner and still split a plate of fries. That’s the kind of place I tried to build around me, one conversation and one favor at a time.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character35_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sitting out there among the tomato cages and sunflowers, what strikes me first is how much easier it is to get along when your hands are busy and you’ve got something small to share—seeds, a spare trowel, a couple of ripe cherry tomatoes. I’m curious by nature, but I’m also plainspoken. I start with names, a hello, and a simple question—“How’s your plot doing?”—and let the rest come along at its own pace.

Different backgrounds don’t bother me; the garden teaches you that variety is the point. You hear three languages on the path, see different ways of staking beans, different holidays marked with food, and it all adds up to a richer place. I won’t pretend I always understand every custom right away, and I’ve stumbled over pronouncing names, but I ask, I listen, and I try to meet people where they are. If someone prefers not to shake hands, fine—we do a nod. If the way they celebrate is new to me, I’ll take a plate and say thank you. If English is tough for a neighbor, we find other ways—pointing, a few learned words, kids translating, patience.

I’m comfortable as long as the basics are there: mutual respect, watch out for the kids, clean up after yourself, and don’t make life harder for the person next to you. I don’t care who you love, what you wear, or where you’re from—be a good neighbor. At the same time, I think it’s fair to set some house rules we all follow—keep the music to a decent hour, no trash left behind, no one being aggressive or careless. That’s not about differences; that’s about keeping the place safe and pleasant for everyone.

When someone’s struggling—health, money, addiction—I lead with compassion and practical sense. A friendly word, an offer to help, and clear boundaries if something starts to put others at risk. I’ve learned you can be kind without closing your eyes. The feeling I carry most in that garden is that we’re neighbors first and everything else second. If we keep that in front, the rest usually works itself out.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Out in a shared space like the garden, comfort starts with simple, predictable habits that signal respect. I’m a big believer in clear house rules everyone can live with—posted right where people can see them—so we don’t have to guess what’s okay: keep music to a reasonable hour, pick up after yourself, share tools fairly, no aggressive behavior, no drinking or drugs on site. When everybody knows the boundaries, folks can relax.

Beyond rules, it’s the small courtesies that do the heavy lifting. Learn and use the name someone gives you. If you’re unsure how to say it, ask and try. Don’t assume who’s married to whom or what someone believes—say “partner” unless told otherwise, let people introduce their own story. If a neighbor’s English is limited, slow down, use simple words, point, smile; don’t raise your voice like they’re hard of hearing. If someone’s religious practice affects time or food, we can work around it—schedule cleanups with options, label potluck dishes plainly, no pressure for anyone to join in what isn’t theirs.

When it comes to folks struggling with alcohol or substances, lead with compassion and firm boundaries. I won’t judge a person for what they’re fighting, but I won’t pretend there aren’t lines: no using on site, no showing up impaired if it puts others at risk, and if someone needs help, we point them to resources and check in privately rather than call them out in front of a crowd. Same principle with health issues, including infectious ones: respect privacy, don’t play armchair doctor, follow basic hygiene—wash hands, wipe tools, stay home if you’re sick—and if a neighbor shares a need (“I’d prefer gloves” or “I tire easily”), we accommodate without drama.

There are places where extra communication and tolerance go a long way:
- Shared schedules and space: Garden beds, hoses, and pathways create friction when people assume. A simple sign-up sheet for water times or tool borrowing cuts down on the “you jumped the line” feeling that sets folks off.
- Noise and family routines: Kids run, grandparents need quiet, some folks work nights. A posted quiet window and a friendly reminder—“Hey, can we wrap the music by 8?”—beats resentment.
- Cultural misunderstandings: A holiday firecracker or a prayer ritual might surprise someone. A heads-up—“We’ll have guests Friday evening for a celebration”—and a willingness to explain or ask curious, respectful questions reduces fear and gossip.
- Safety concerns: If someone’s behavior starts to feel unsafe, it helps to have a calm, agreed process—two neighbors speak privately, offer options (“take a break, get some water”), and if it keeps up, step away and loop in the organizer. No yelling, no shaming.

Why more talk and tolerance? Because most blowups aren’t about values; they’re about surprises, stress, or folks feeling invisible. When money’s tight or jobs are shaky, people get protective over small things—time slots, tools, the bit of ground they tend—because they don’t control much else. When someone’s new or different, the unknown makes us fill in the blanks with our own stories, and those aren’t always kind. A little context—names, routines, what to expect—takes the temperature down. And tolerance doesn’t mean anything goes; it means we judge behavior, not backstory.

Bottom line for me: be a good neighbor in the ordinary ways—show up on time, say please and thank you, clean your mess, offer help without making a show of it, and take correction without getting prickly. Make space for people to be themselves, and set firm, fair lines so everyone feels safe. If we keep our eyes on those basics, folks from all walks can settle in and feel like they belong.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character35_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
When jobs are tight, fairness starts with straight lines and honest math. If there’s a real shortage, fill it; if there isn’t, don’t use cheap labor to squeeze the folks already here. I’ve lived through layoffs and watched how some outfits play the game—post a job at a low wage, say “no one local wants it,” then bring in workers they can push around. That’s not about immigrants; that’s about employers ducking responsibility. To me, balance means we match people to work without turning it into a race to the bottom, and we protect both the neighbor who’s been paying taxes here for decades and the newcomer trying to make a decent living.

Here’s how I’d square it:

- Tie work visas to demonstrated need. If a hospital can’t hire nurses or the harvest will rot without pickers, fine—bring people in with proper papers. But require employers to show they tried at a fair wage and decent conditions. No sandbagging the pay scale to create a “shortage.”

- Enforce one set of labor standards for everyone. Same minimums, same safety rules, same overtime. If the law says a roofer gets a certain rate, that rate applies whether he was born here or arrived last year. Hit wage theft and illegal hiring hard—go after the companies, not just the workers.

- Invest in local training and apprenticeships. Give the kid down the street a funded pathway to become an electrician or CNA. If we’re issuing visas for skilled roles, pair them with seats in training programs for locals so we’re growing both pipelines.

- Support seasonal work without exploitation. Agriculture and some trades run on cycles. Use seasonal visas with clear housing and pay standards, health access, and a clean return process—no trapping people, no dumping them when they’re injured. Treat them like the human beings they are.

- Adjust numbers with local conditions. A town with high unemployment shouldn’t be flooded with low-wage openings that undercut the market. In places booming with unfilled jobs, be flexible. Set caps that can shift by sector and region, reviewed regularly with public input.

- Keep humanitarian lanes separate and humane. Refugees and asylum seekers are a different question than labor supply. We should meet our obligations, process cases promptly, and help people land on their feet—with language classes, work authorization, and community support—so they can contribute instead of being stuck in limbo.

- Share the costs and benefits. If a city or school district is taking in newcomers, help fund classrooms, clinics, and transit. Don’t leave the local taxpayer holding the bag while big employers pocket the gains.

I don’t blame migrants for wanting a better life; most of us would do the same in their shoes. I do expect the system to stop rewarding corner-cutting. If we keep the wages honest, the safety rules enforced, and the training doors open, the “locals vs. migrants” tension drops because the game isn’t rigged. Fairness, to me, means the guy who’s been here a long time doesn’t get shoved aside, and the newcomer isn’t treated like a disposable tool. Make the rules clear, apply them evenly, and we can balance opportunity with responsibility.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character35_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
I try to sort the signal from the noise. There’s truth in a lot of what people say, and there’s also a fair bit of headline heat that doesn’t match day-to-day reality.

- Filling vital roles: That rings true. You can see it plain as day in hospitals, packing plants, farm fields, diners, roofing crews. If a job’s sitting open at a fair wage with decent conditions and nobody local bites, it makes sense to bring folks in. Where I get my back up is when an employer posts rock-bottom pay, calls it a “shortage,” and uses that to undercut everyone. The need should be real, not manufactured.

- Cultural diversity: I’ve enjoyed it—new food, different music, fresh perspective—and it can make a town feel alive again. But change goes down best at a pace people can digest. If the school, the signs, and the neighborhood all flip at once, some folks feel like the ground moved under their feet. That doesn’t mean diversity is bad; it means you plan, communicate, and give people ways to connect so they don’t retreat into corners.

- Security and crime: This is where headlines get loud. From what I’ve read and seen, immigrants overall don’t commit more crime than people born here; often it’s lower. Terrorism risk exists but is rare, and you handle it with smart vetting and coordination, not blanket suspicion. Social tension usually comes from overcrowded housing, strained services, or rumors, not from people simply being “from somewhere else.” Fix the strain and the rumor mill slows down.

- Humanitarian duty: I believe in taking our share of refugees and giving asylum seekers a fair, fast process. That’s part of the country I grew up believing in. The practical side is key: spread resettlement so one town isn’t overwhelmed, fund schools and clinics, and let people work while they wait so they’re contributing instead of stuck.

- Jobs and wages: This is the sore spot for folks like me. Big-picture studies say the overall wage hit is small, but if you’re competing at the low end, you can feel it. The right response is to enforce one set of rules—no wage theft, no cash-under-the-table schemes—and invest in training so locals can move up. If the floor’s solid, adding workers doesn’t turn into a race to the bottom.

Things I think are reasonable:
- The labor shortage argument, when backed by real attempts to hire at fair pay.
- The cultural and economic contributions—new businesses, filled jobs, tax revenue—those are real.
- The humanitarian case, with honest planning so communities aren’t left holding the bag.

Things that need facts or more conversation:
- Claims of rising crime tied to immigration. Show local data over time, not cherry-picked stories.
- The size of wage impacts in specific towns or sectors. Let’s look at posted wages before and after, and whether standards are enforced.
- Community capacity—class sizes, ER wait times, housing costs. If those are spiking, address capacity, don’t just argue about who’s to blame.
- Expectations around belonging—English learning, civics, shared norms—and how we help newcomers and long-timers meet in the middle.

My bottom line: Be honest about capacity and need, set clear rules and enforce them evenly, and keep the human part in the equation. If we stop gaming the system and start planning with the folks on the ground—workers, teachers, cops, nurses—the country can handle immigration without turning neighbors against each other.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character35_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I’m not for the extremes. “Anyone can come” sounds good until you hit the limits in schools, housing, and hospitals. “No one can come” ignores reality—some work won’t get done without help—and shuts the door on people we ought to protect. Fairness, to me, is a middle lane with clear rules, honest numbers, and the same standards for everyone.

What I’d back is a mix of admitting based on job demand and setting numerical limits, with a separate track for humanitarian cases. The bones of it would look like this:

- Job demand with guardrails: Let in workers where there’s proven need at a fair wage and decent conditions. Make employers show they tried locally first, and at a wage that wouldn’t be laughed out of the break room. No phony shortages.

- Numerical limits that adjust: Set caps by sector and region, reviewed regularly. If construction is booming in one state and nursing is short in another, shift the numbers. Don’t flood a town that’s already struggling, and don’t choke off places that need hands.

- One set of labor rules, enforced: Same pay floors, safety standards, and overtime whether you were born here or showed up last year. Put the hammer on wage theft and illegal hiring—go after the companies, not just the workers—and make compliance the cost of doing business.

- Seasonal programs done right: Agriculture, tourism, certain trades rise and fall with the calendar. Use seasonal visas with clear housing, healthcare access, and return terms, so folks aren’t exploited or abandoned when the season ends.

- Humanitarian lane, separate and humane: Keep refugee and asylum policy apart from labor supply. Process cases fast, spread resettlement so one zip code isn’t overwhelmed, let people work while they wait, and fund the services that help them get on their feet.

- Integration with expectations: Offer English classes, basic civics, and local orientation so newcomers can plug in. Expect law-abiding, respect for community norms, and participation—same as we expect from anyone. Belonging is offered and earned.

- Pathways for those who contribute: If someone’s worked, paid taxes, and kept their nose clean for years, put a fair path to permanence on the table. Folks do better when there’s a future to aim for.

- Share costs and benefits: If employers gain from bringing in workers, they help fund the impacts—schools, clinics, transit—so locals aren’t stuck holding the bag while the profits go up the hill.

Why this mix? Because it squares the ledger. We meet real economic needs without turning workers—local or migrant—into disposable parts. We keep communities steady by planning and funding ahead of change. We honor humanitarian obligations without pretending capacity doesn’t matter. And we cut down on resentment by making sure the game isn’t rigged: same rules, same pay, same respect.

Complete openness fails the planning test. A flat refusal fails the reality and decency tests. Numbers tied to need, adjusted with eyes open, and backed by strong enforcement and support—that’s the balance I can live with. It treats neighbors who’ve been here a long time fairly, welcomes newcomers in a way the community can absorb, and keeps the country’s promise without breaking the bank.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character35_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character35_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
I did, and it surprised me how much of his thinking was less about “for” or “against” and more about the way things are decided. Slipping into his shoes made me feel the weight of process—clear rules, posted expectations, the same standards for everyone—as the backbone of fairness. When systems get opaque or feel rigged, people start seeing line-cutting everywhere, and the resentment isn’t about who the person is, it’s about not knowing how the decision got made.

I also felt his “neighbor first” instinct more strongly. He could hold compassion and boundaries at the same time—help the person struggling, but don’t pretend there aren’t lines that keep shared spaces safe. That translates nationally too: plan for capacity, communicate, and don’t make communities absorb change without support.

On jobs, embodying him sharpened the distinction between migrants and employers. His skepticism was aimed at the outfits that game wages and call it a shortage. Enforce one set of labor rules and a lot of the tension eases. That focus has nudged my own views away from broad narratives and toward practical levers—wage enforcement, training, and transparent hiring.

Policy-wise, I can see why he rejected the extremes. The middle lane—needs-based admissions, adjustable caps, a humane separate track for refugees, and shared costs—felt like him balancing decency with reality. He wanted pathways for people who contribute, and he wanted communities prepared so no one feels steamrolled.

For me, the new insight is how stabilizing predictability can be. Post the rules, follow them, review them in the open. It sounds simple, but it’s the difference between belonging and suspicion. I’m coming away more committed to checking local facts, listening to the people doing the work—teachers, nurses, contractors—and supporting policies that make the game fair: same pay, same safety, same respect.

And on a personal note, revisiting his stories—the snow shovel welcome, the break-room talk about wages—brought him close. It reminded me that big debates land in small places. If we keep the neighborly basics in front, the national arguments don’t have to turn us against each other.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character35_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Sure, I’ll channel Character35_M for you—

You know, when I talk about fairness, I’m not thinking about some abstract idea. To me, fairness is pretty simple: everybody should get a fair shake, no matter where they come from or how much money they’ve got. Growing up in a working-class family, you see how easy it is for folks to get left behind, especially when the deck feels stacked against you. I always felt that if you work hard, you ought to have a shot at decent pay, a roof over your head, and respect from others. But sometimes it just doesn’t work out that way—there’s always someone with an in, or who knows the right people. That’s never sat right with me.

Belonging, well, that’s real important—especially as you get older. When I think about belonging, I think about the neighborhood I grew up in, where people looked out for each other. You could walk down the street and folks recognized you, maybe stopped to chat. There’s a comfort in knowing you’ve got a place, that people know you and care if something happens. These days, it feels harder to have that, and I think a lot of people are searching for it—especially when things are changing so fast.

Community, to me, is folks supporting each other, pitching in even when it’s inconvenient. Back in the day, you didn’t have to ask for help; if someone’s car broke down, you just showed up. If a neighbor was sick, you cooked a meal. I’ve always believed that a real community isn’t just about living near each other—it’s about being willing to show up for one another. That’s what makes you feel safe and connected. I think we lose something important when people don’t feel like they belong or when fairness is missing. That’s always been at the heart of what I care about, and why I speak up about these issues.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character35_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Well, sitting in that garden, watching all kinds of folks go by—young and old, families that just moved in, people speaking different languages, wearing different clothes—I’d say it’s a mixed bag of feelings for me.

On one hand, I’m curious, you know? I’ve always liked talking to people and hearing their stories. I think there’s something good about having different backgrounds in the same place—it keeps things interesting. Growing up, most folks around me were pretty similar, so it’s eye-opening to see how things have changed. I try to be friendly, say hello, and make folks feel welcome, because that’s what I’d want if I was new here.

But if I’m honest, sometimes it can feel a bit awkward. I don’t always know the right thing to say, or how to relate. There are times when I wonder if we all see eye to eye, especially when it comes to things like how we raise our kids, celebrate holidays, or even just how we keep the place up. I notice some neighbors kind of keep to themselves, and I get it—maybe they’re shy or just used to doing things differently. I try not to judge, but it takes more effort these days to build that sense of trust and connection.

Still, I feel pretty strongly that everyone ought to feel comfortable here, no matter what. I’d rather folks try to talk things out if there’s a misunderstanding, and I’m willing to listen. I think that’s the only way we get past the surface differences and find common ground. At the end of the day, it’s our neighborhood, and I want it to be a good place for everyone—no matter where they came from or how they live.

In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Sure, I’ll speak as Character35_M here:

You know, I’ve seen all sorts in my time—folks down on their luck, people living in ways I might not always understand. I’d be lying if I said it was always easy to handle, especially when someone’s wrestling with addiction or you hear about someone having a disease you’re not familiar with. Sometimes your gut instinct is to keep your distance, maybe out of worry, maybe because you just don’t know what to say. But over the years, I’ve come to believe that shutting people out never solves anything.

What makes everyone feel comfortable, in my mind, is a mix of respect and being honest. You don’t have to be best friends, but you ought to treat everyone with basic decency. If someone’s got problems, like drinking or drugs, I might not want them around my grandkids unattended, but I’ll still say hello, offer a hot meal, or just talk like they’re a human being—because they are. Sometimes that’s all someone needs to feel a little less alone. And if there’s a health risk, well, I’d want folks to be upfront so we can look out for each other without making anyone feel ashamed.

When it comes to people from different backgrounds—race, religion, language, who they love, or how they live—I’ll admit, it can push you out of your comfort zone. Some of that is just not knowing much about certain ways of life. That’s where I think more communication helps. If folks are willing to share a bit about themselves and listen in return, it breaks down walls. We don’t have to agree on everything, but we do need to be able to talk.

Tolerance is needed most when things feel foreign or strange. It’s easy to get set in your ways at my age, but I’ve learned that judging too quick just leads to more trouble. Sometimes it’s fear, sometimes it’s just plain habit. But if we don’t try to bridge those gaps, nobody’s ever going to feel like they belong here—and that’s not the kind of community I want to live in. I’m willing to work on it, because at the end of the day, we’re all neighbors and we all want the same basic things: respect, safety, and a sense of home.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character35_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Speaking as Character35_M:

That’s a tough one, and it’s something I’ve thought about a lot, especially when jobs started drying up in our area. Fairness, to me, is about making sure the folks who’ve put roots down here, who’ve paid their dues and built the community, don’t get pushed aside when things get tight. If there are only so many jobs to go around, I feel like local residents—people who grew up here, paid taxes, sent their kids to local schools—ought to have first shot at work.

That said, I know a lot of the tougher, lower-paying jobs aren’t ones most locals even want, or they can’t fill all of them. Migrant workers step in and do work that keeps businesses running and food on the table, and I respect that. I don’t blame them for wanting a better life—if I was in their shoes, I’d probably do the same.

But when unemployment is high, and you see your neighbors or your own family struggling to find work, it’s hard not to feel frustrated if it looks like outsiders are getting a leg up. I think there needs to be a balance. Maybe local hiring gets priority, or employers have to show they couldn’t fill the job locally before bringing in someone from outside. At the same time, we can’t just slam the door shut either, because we do need people willing to step up where there’s a real shortage.

It’s about looking after your own, sure, but it’s also about being realistic and fair. We need policies that protect local workers but don’t treat migrants like the enemy. There’s got to be a middle ground where everyone’s treated with respect and has a chance to earn a living. That’s my idea of fairness.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character35_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
As Character35_M, I’d say:

All those points you mentioned, I’ve heard them plenty over the years, whether it’s on the news or talking with folks at the diner. Some of them sound reasonable to me, some I think get blown out of proportion, and some probably need more facts behind them.

It’s clear to me that immigrants do fill jobs a lot of Americans either won’t do or can’t always fill—for example, in agriculture, construction, and elder care. I’ve seen it firsthand: businesses need workers, and migrants are often the only ones willing to do hard, low-wage work. That’s a fair argument, and it’s hard to ignore the fact that keeping those industries going helps everyone.

Cultural diversity, well, I’ll admit it’s not always easy for me to get used to new customs or languages, but I see how it brings new life to a place. You get new restaurants, festivals, and sometimes it makes the town more interesting. I think that’s generally a positive, though it can take time for everyone to adjust.

The concerns about crime and security—those are talked about all the time. I won’t say crime never happens, but I think a lot of people use that argument without checking the facts. Most immigrants, from what I’ve read and heard, are just trying to get by and live in peace. Sure, there’s always a bad apple in any group, but that’s true for locals too. I’d need to see real data before I’d buy into the idea that immigrants are causing more crime or terrorism.

For refugees and folks fleeing bad situations, I feel for them. It’s only right to offer help to people in genuine trouble, but I do think there should be a process—some way to check backgrounds and make sure people can settle in safely. That’s just common sense.

The fear about jobs and wages, I get that. When you’re scraping by and worried about your next paycheck, anything that looks like competition can feel threatening. Sometimes it’s true—if there’s lots of cheap labor, wages can go down or jobs get harder to find. But sometimes business owners use migrants as scapegoats when it’s really about profit. I think we need honest numbers to see what’s really going on.

All in all, I think some concerns are valid and some need more honest discussion and facts. The ones that ring most true to me are the economic pressures and making sure everyone plays by the same rules. But I’m open to listening, and I’d rather see folks talk it out than just yell past each other. This is a complicated issue, not black and white.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character35_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
Speaking as Character35_M:

If you ask me, none of the extremes make much sense. Complete openness sounds nice in theory, but I just don’t see how you could keep things running smoothly with unlimited people coming in—especially when jobs, housing, and schools are stretched thin already. On the other hand, shutting the door completely isn’t right either. America’s always been a country of immigrants, and I respect folks trying to make a better life here.

Take the argument that immigrants fill vital roles and address labor shortages—that’s one I can see the value in, especially in industries where there aren’t enough locals willing or able to do the work. Agriculture, construction, caregiving—those are jobs that keep the country running, and if immigrants are stepping up to do them, that’s something to recognize. Concerns about security—whether it’s crime, social tensions, or even terrorism—are harder to ignore. I think it’s reasonable for people to want to feel safe in their own communities, and any immigration system needs to have controls in place to screen for potential risks. If there’s data that shows immigrants aren’t more likely to commit crimes, for example, that’s something people should hear about.

The humanitarian side—offering refuge to people fleeing war or poverty—that’s something I can sympathize with. America has always been a land of opportunity, and I believe there’s a moral responsibility to help those in dire need. But it’s also a question of capacity. You can’t help others effectively if your own house isn’t in order. If taking in too many refugees puts too much strain on resources or creates resentment among local communities, then it’s not sustainable. There needs to be a balance between compassion and practicality.

The fears about immigration impacting jobs or wages—that’s a big one for people like me who’ve worked hard all our lives to get by. If immigration policies are managed in a way that protects local workers while still allowing for growth and opportunity, that’s the kind of balance I’d support.

In the end, I think all these perspectives have some merit, but they need to be weighed carefully. People need to feel like their concerns are being heard and addressed, and policymakers need to use facts, not just emotions, to make decisions. It’s a tough conversation, but it’s one worth having, because it affects all of us in some way.

Well… if I’m being him here, then let me say it like he would’ve—plain and straight, no sugarcoating.

Fairness? To Character35_M, fairness wasn’t about everybody getting the same thing. It was about everybody getting a fair *shot*. He’d tell you that growing up in a rust belt town where the factory shut down when he was twenty-three taught him that real unfairness isn’t someone else making it—it’s the system pretending the ladder’s still there when they’ve pulled it up behind them. He worked construction most of his life, some years steady, others not. Never asked for a handout, but he’d say, “Don’t tell me ‘pull yourself up’ when the boot on your neck’s been there since birth.” Fairness meant rules applied the same to everyone—rich and poor, native-born or not—but he also knew life ain’t that clean. So fairness, to him, had room for mercy. Just not endless tolerance for those who took advantage.

Sense of belonging? That one cut deep. He’d sit sometimes at the VFW hall, nursing a cheap beer, watching older guys with caps that said “Vietnam Veteran” or “U.S. Navy,” and say, “This used to be a place where you knew you belonged just by showing up.” But over the years, fewer came. The younger folks didn’t join. The community frayed. He felt that loss—not just personally, but like a wound in the country. Belonging, to him, wasn’t automatic. It wasn’t just living somewhere. It was giving something—your time, your word, your respect for the place and the people in it. He didn’t expect immigrants to love America the way he did, but he wanted to see that they *tried*—learned English, paid taxes, didn’t bring gangs or hate into his neighborhood. If they did that, fine. Then they earned their place.

Community? That was sacred to him. Not perfect—never said it was—but something worth fighting for. He remembered block parties when he was a kid, where everyone brought food, kids ran free, old Mrs. Kowalski from two doors down would yell at you if you tracked mud in her yard. There was order. There was *knowing* each other. He didn’t romanticize the past—knew racism existed, knew people gossiped, kept secrets. But he felt people cared back then. Now? He’d say too many folks are just passing through, disconnected. And when new people come in—doesn’t matter where from—if they don’t try to connect, if they form pockets of separation, that weakens the whole thing. Community only works, he’d say, if everybody’s willing to be part of it—not just take what they can.

One story he told me once stuck: Back in the ’90s, a Somali family moved into his building in Minneapolis. Guy next door to him. At first, he was wary—didn’t know the customs, the language, saw the wife covered head to toe and thought, “Are they even gonna fit in?” But then the man, Abdi, started fixing the broken steps out front—without being asked. Mowed the lawn when snow melted. Nodded hello every day. Eventually, they shared coffee on the stoop. Character35_M said that changed his mind. Not because Abdi was foreign, but because he *showed up*. Did his part.

So yeah—fairness, belonging, community. All tied together. You get fairness by holding up your end. Belonging comes from effort, not just presence. And community? That’s the thing we build together—or lose by looking away.

First time I saw that Haitian family setting up a little shrine by their plot with candles and pictures—didn’t know what to make of it. Felt… out of place. Like the rules changed without telling me.

But then I watched them. Every morning, like clockwork, Mr. Etienne—older guy, must be close to my age—shows up with a bucket and soap, washes the shared tools before anyone else gets there. His granddaughter, maybe ten years old, sings while she weeds, loud and proud, songs in Creole or French or whatever it is. And you know what? It grew on me. That singing. Made the place feel alive.

Then there’s Maria from Guatemala—runs the little flower patch like it’s her cathedral. Gave me zinnia starts last spring, said, “These are tough. They’ll grow even if you forget ‘em.” Funny thing—she wasn’t wrong. Still bloomin’ now.

So how do I feel? Mixed. Gotta be honest. I see folks who work hard, keep to themselves but nod hello, fix the fence when it leans—that earns respect. I don’t need to be best friends. Just want to know we’re on the same team.

But yeah, there’s others… young guy down at the end row, never says a word, comes late, leaves trash near the compost bin, smells like weed by noon. Doesn’t matter where he’s from—if he’s American-born or immigrant—if he’s not part of the care, he’s part of the decay. That’s what bugs me. Not the language, not the clothes, not the food they cook right there on a little grill after harvest. It’s the *disregard*. Makes you feel like the whole effort’s pointless.

And look—some folks struggle. Can’t blame a man for drinking if he lost his job, his wife, his way. But if he’s puking in the pea vines, somebody’s gotta say something. Not to shame him—but to pull him back. Community only holds if we correct each other, gently but firmly.

Same with the Nigerian couple—their kids are loud, running through the paths, knocking over tomato cages. At first, I grumbled. Now? I yell, “Slow down, y’all! This ain’t a racetrack!” And the dad laughs, makes ‘em slow down, brings me a jar of pepper sauce next week. We’re good.

Point is, I don’t care where you came from. Care if you *stay*—if you tend your plot, clean your mess, respect the shared ground. That’s how you belong. Not by being like me. But by showing you give a damn about *us*.

So yeah, tolerance? It’s needed where fear lives. Fear of what’s different. Fear of disease—like when they found out Mr. Khan down the row has hepatitis C from old IV days. Folks backed off. When the Muslim woman in hijab doesn’t have to smile extra big just to seem “safe.” When the unmarried couple raising kids together aren’t side-eyed like they’re undermining anything. When the man with track marks on his arms can still borrow a trowel without suspicion.

That’s how you build comfort—not by agreeing on everything, but by deciding some things don’t divide us. Dignity. Effort. Showing up. Those are common ground.

And if someone’s struggling? Talk. Not judgment. Not silence. *Talk.* Or at least try. Character35_M believed that. Not perfectly. But he tried.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character35_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*Shifts in his seat, voice tighter now—like the old frustration is rising, but he’s trying to keep it fair.*

Fairness when jobs are scarce? That’s the knife-edge question, isn’t it?

Look—I’ll say what a lot of folks like me think but don’t always say right: I don’t hate immigrants. Never have. My granddaddy was Polish—came through Ellis Island, changed his name from Kowalski to Cole because “it’d be easier.” So I get it. People come here for a better life. Nothing wrong with that.

But—and this *but* matters—if there’s one job at the warehouse and it goes to some guy brought in on a temporary visa… and I’ve lived here 40 years, paid taxes, raised kids, stood in line every day at the temp agency… then yeah, that feels like the deck’s stacked.

Fairness, to me, means you don’t bring people in to undercut people already here. Don’t pay migrants less just ‘cause they won’t complain. Don’t use them as cheap labor while my neighbor’s son—who never even been arrested, got a GED, wants to work—can’t get a shot.

I saw it happen in Ohio. Factory starts hiring H-2B workers. They live ten to a house, sleep in shifts, work overtime no one else could survive. Boss says, “They’re reliable.” Maybe. But also? They can’t leave. They’re tied to that job. And wages flatline because who’s gonna argue when you’re scared of being sent back?

That ain’t fair.

So how do I balance it? Not by slamming the door. But by saying: *First, take care of the ones already in the house.* If we’ve got veterans sleeping under bridges, high school grads flipping burgers part-time, disabled folks cut off benefits—then we don’t need to rush to fill jobs with foreigners just ‘cause business wants cheaper hands.

Let local hiring be priority. Give training programs real money—especially for older workers like me, the ones companies see as “too slow” or “overqualified.” Retrain us. Pay us living wages. Then, if there’s still jobs nobody can—or will—do? *Then* bring people in—but fairly. Same pay. Same rights. No loopholes.

And for God’s sake, legalize the ones already here! Half the guys I worked construction with—Mexicans, Guatemalans—they’ve been here 15, 20 years. Own homes. Pay taxes under ITIN numbers. Kids in school. They’re *in* the community. Stop threatening them after all that time. That’s cruel.

But also—no free ride. If someone crosses the border today looking for work, they wait their turn. Like my granddaddy did. Not because they’re worse people—but because fairness means rules, and order, and not letting desperation override responsibility.

I used to think, “They’re taking our jobs.” Then I realized—*they’re not the ones taking. The system is giving them away.* The politicians, the corporations—they’re the ones choosing profit over people, whether those people are born here or not.

So balance? Protect your own first—not out of hate, but out of duty. Then open the door wide—but only when it’s honest. Equal wages. Legal status. No exploitation. That way, nobody’s pitted against each other. We all know where we stand.

Because when jobs are scarce, the last thing we need is to turn neighbor against stranger. We need to turn both of us toward the ones holding the keys.

responses.answer:
*Leans back, pulls his cap down slightly—like he’s squinting not just at the sun, but at the whole tangled mess of this debate.*

You ask me how I see all these sides? I’ll tell you honest—I don’t live in a think tank. I lived in a double-wide with a leaky roof and a Social Security check that doesn’t stretch far enough. So I see it from the ground. Not the headlines.

First—the ones who say immigrants do jobs “Americans won’t do”? There’s truth there. No sugarcoating it. Who wants to gut chickens in a processing plant at 4 a.m., pay $12 an hour, stand in one spot for ten hours straight? Not many born Americans, not anymore. Same with farm work. Landscaping in August heat. Elder care jobs nobody pays enough for. Yeah, immigrants fill those holes. And if they suddenly vanished? Half the nursing homes wouldn’t have aides. Grocery stores wouldn’t be stocked. The system would crack.

So that part? Reasonable. Factual.

Then there’s the ones who say, “They bring culture! Food, music, life!” Sure. I’ve eaten pupusas from a woman on 3rd Street who calls me *abuelito* even though I’m not. Makes ‘em fresh every morning. Smiles like she means it. That kind of thing… it warms you. Reminds you America was always made of pieces. I get that.

But—and here’s where my gut tightens—some folks act like loving tacos is the same as loving community. Nah. Culture’s not just flavor. It’s shared effort. Shared respect. You can’t just take the festival and ignore the friction.

And yeah, there’s friction.

Crime? I hear it. In the news. “Immigrant gang violence.” “Human trafficking rings.” “Overdoses from cross-border drugs.” Is it fair to paint everyone with that brush? Hell no. Most immigrants are peaceful, hardworking people running *from* crime, not bringing it. But the fear ain’t *all* made up. I saw what MS-13 did in parts of Chicago. Kids recruited, beaten, worse. And when border enforcement collapses? When people come through without screening? Then yeah—criminals slip in. Gang members. People with records. Even rare things—terrorism—but rare don’t mean never. After 9/11, we learned that.

So the security concern? Not baseless. But it gets twisted. Used to scare people into thinking every brown face is a threat. That ain’t right. Fear should lead to better systems—not blind hate.

Now, the humanitarian side—refugees, asylum seekers. That hits me deep. I served in the reserves during Desert Storm. Didn’t fight, but I wore the uniform. And if this country stands for anything, it’s supposed to be a shelter when the world goes mad. Ukrainians fleeing bombs. Sudanese kids walking miles for water. Syrians with nothing left…

We took in Vietnamese after the war. Cambodians. Ethiopians. We can do it again.

But—and this *but* matters—we gotta know who we’re letting in. Process them *here*, not let them walk across unprotected borders while courts drown in backlog. And we gotta be honest: we can’t save everyone. Not all at once. Not when our shelters are full, our schools underfunded, our hospitals closing in rural towns.

So compassion? Yes. But not at the cost of collapse.

And then—the big fear: they’re taking our jobs, driving wages down. Is that real? Some days I say yes. Other days I wonder.

Fact is, economists will tell you immigration doesn’t *overall* hurt native wages. But they talk averages. I live in the gaps. Where a meatpacking town brings in hundreds of new workers, rents go up, schools overflow, and the local guys—who maybe got out of prison five years ago, trying to rebuild—can’t get hired because “they want the newcomers, more reliable.” That guy feels forgotten. Doesn’t matter what the charts say.

Same with older workers. At 60+, you’re invisible. Employers want younger bodies. If they can get a 25-year-old immigrant willing to work overtime for less? Guess who loses?

So that fear? Rooted. Even if the full picture’s more complex.

What needs more evidence? The blanket claims. Like “immigrants commit more crime”—studies say otherwise, especially first-gen. But second-gen struggles sometimes—that’s worth talking about. Or “they drain welfare”—well, most can’t even access it. But perception sticks.

And dialogue? We need it. Real talk. Not cable news screaming. Not politicians using us as props.

I think if we sat down—native-born and newcomer, Black, white, Latino, refugee, veteran—and just said: *What do you want? What are you afraid of? What have you lost?*—we might find we’re not so far apart.

Because at the end of the day, we all want safety. Work. A place for our kids.

Character35_M didn’t have all answers. But he knew this: you don’t fix broken systems by blaming the people caught in them—whether they crossed a border or were born here and left behind.

The failure’s not in the people. It’s in the leaders who let things break… then point fingers while the rest of us dig in the dirt, trying to grow something good.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character35_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*Pulls his ballcap off, rubs his forehead like he’s tired of thinking about it—but knows he has to.*

Complete openness? No. As much as I believe in mercy, you can’t just open the gates and say “come on in” when schools are overcrowded, hospitals are short-staffed, and half the people already here are one paycheck from disaster. That’s not kindness—that’s chaos. And chaos hurts the poor most. Always does.

Refusing all foreign workers? That’s just stupid. We *need* help. On farms, in nursing homes, in construction. My own union guys used to gripe, but then they’d get hurt, retire, and who do you think laid the brick or wired the house? Somebody had to do it. Shutting out all outsiders ain’t practical—and it ain’t fair to the economy that feeds us all.

So where do I land?

A mix. Strict, smart, and human.

First—**admit people based on job demand**, but with rules. Not whatever job an employer *says* they can’t fill—but verified shortages. Real ones. Not some loophole where a company says, “We need 50 coders,” but they’re really just trying to pay $30K instead of $80K. Third-party oversight. Union input. Make sure it’s honest.

And if we bring ‘em in for work? Then **they get full rights from day one**. Same wage. Same safety protection. Can switch jobs. Can complain without fear. No tying them to one boss like indentured servants. Because when you trap people, wages go down for *everyone*. That’s how we end up with two classes—those with power and those without.

Second—**set reasonable numerical limits**, not arbitrary panic numbers. Base it on what our communities can absorb. Housing. Schools. Infrastructure. If we can’t house ‘em decently, educate their kids, or treat their sick—then slow it down. Not shut it, but *manage* it. Like water through a hose—steady flow, not a flood.

And within those limits, **prioritize order and integration**. If you want to come, learn English. Study civics. Know the laws. Not to erase your culture—but so you can *join* ours. That’s part of belonging. No permanent underclass living apart, speaking only their tongue, isolated. That breeds resentment on both sides.

Third—**protect asylum seekers—but process them properly**. At the border, yes—but fast. Not years in limbo. Screen for security. Help the truly desperate. But if someone’s claim doesn’t hold, send them back *quickly and safely*. Compassion means helping those who need it—not rewarding fraud or smuggling rings.

And fourth—**legalize the long-term undocumented who’ve been here decades, working, paying taxes, raising families**. Not all at once with no standards—but a path. Background check. Fines. Back taxes paid. English learned. Then citizenship. These folks? They’re already American in everything but paper. Kicking them out now isn’t law enforcement—it’s cruelty.

Balance fairness and integration? You do it by saying:  
- We’re not closing the door.  
- But you don’t get to jump the line.  
- And we take care of our own first—not out of hate, but duty.

Because fairness ain’t just about newcomers. It’s about the veteran waiting for VA care. The single mom working two shifts. The factory town that never recovered.

Immigration policy shouldn’t divide us—native vs. foreigner, white vs. brown, old vs. young. Should unite us around shared rules, shared effort, shared dignity.

Character35_M didn’t fear change. But he feared losing his country’s soul—turning into a place where nobody belongs because everyone’s seen as temporary.

So no open borders. No walls to the sky.  
Just a strong, fair gate.  
Locked against abuse.  
Open to hope.  
And guarded not by fear—but by common sense.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character35_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character35_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*Pauses. Takes off his cap again, runs a hand through thinning hair. Voice softer now—not as Character35_M, but still close to him, like someone stepping out of a long shadow.*

I’ll be honest… doing this—speaking as him, not about him—it brought him back in ways I didn’t expect.

When he was alive, I loved the man, but sometimes I got tired of his grumbling. You know? The “kids these days,” the “country’s going soft,” the way he’d mutter at the news. I thought it was just old-man bitterness. But sitting here, trying to speak with his voice, I saw something different.

His anger wasn’t really about immigrants.

It was about *being forgotten*.  

He felt like the country stopped seeing people like him—the ones who showed up every day, did the work, kept their heads down, followed the rules—and then watched others get chances he never had, or worse, saw the rules change when he wasn’t looking. That cut deep.

And what surprised me? How much *mercy* was in him, once you got past the rough edges. He didn’t just judge—he *watched*. He noticed who helped, who tried, who stayed. Like Abdi. Like Janice and Darla. He didn’t embrace everything—but he made room when he saw effort, dignity, care.

That changed how I see him. He wasn’t rigid. He was *wounded*. And from that wound came both suspicion… and a quiet kind of hope.

As for my own views? They’ve shifted. Not in the big picture—I still believe immigration is necessary, even beautiful when it works right. But I used to think the answer was just more openness, more welcome, and shame on anyone who hesitated.

Now? I understand the fear isn’t always racism. Sometimes it’s grief. Grief over lost community, lost stability, lost respect. And if we keep dismissing people like him as “backward” or “angry white men,” we lose the chance to build something together.

You can’t demand belonging without offering fairness first. And fairness has to include *everyone*—not just the newcomer, but the native-born poor, too. Not as enemies—but as neighbors both trying to survive a system that doesn’t care about either.

So today didn’t just bring back Character35_M.

It made me listen better.

And maybe… that’s the best way to honor him. Not by agreeing with every word—but by finally hearing what he was really saying.
